slides: In this lesson, three more kinds of counting question. At least one, objects that go into boxes, and the most tries we might need.

slides.say: Each one has its own trick, so let's see them one at a time.
Let's start with a tiny case. We toss two coins. In how many outcomes do we get at least one head?
Here are all the outcomes. Head head, head tail, tail head, and tail tail. Two times two is four.
At least one head means one head or two heads. Only tail tail has no head at all.
So the outcomes we want are all of them, minus the one with no head. Four minus one is three.
So at least one is all, minus none. Why? Because the opposite of at least one is none, and none is easy to count.
at: So at least one is all, minus none

slides.say: Now a new example. Two-digit codes from the digits one to five, and digits may repeat. How many codes have at least one five?
at: How many codes have at least one five

slides.say: All the codes first. Five times five is twenty-five.
Now the codes with no five at all. Each digit has only four options, one to four. Four times four is sixteen.
All minus none. Twenty-five minus sixteen is nine.
Let's check with a list. Fifteen, twenty-five, thirty-five, forty-five, and fifty-one up to fifty-five. Nine codes.
Why not count directly? Many students say a five first gives five codes, and a five second gives five more. Five plus five is ten.
But fifty-five was counted twice, once in each group. That's why all minus none is safer.
Now a new kind of question. Two letters, A and B, go into two boxes. A box may get both letters, or none. In how many ways can we do it?
Let's list them. Both letters in box one. A in box one and B in box two. A in box two and B in box one. And both in box two. Four ways.
at: A in box one and B in box two
A in box two and B in box one

slides.say: In stages, who chooses? Each letter chooses a box. Letter A has two options, and letter B has two options. Two times two is four.
So every object is a stage, and each stage has as many options as there are boxes.
Now a new example. Three children each choose one of four ice cream flavours. Two children may choose the same flavour. In how many ways can they choose?
Who chooses? Each child chooses a flavour. So each child is a stage, with four options.
Four times four times four is sixty-four.
The trap is to turn it around. Three times three times three times three is eighty-one. That lets every flavour choose a child, and that's not the story.

slides: If you're not sure which number is the base, try a tiny case you can list, like the two letters and two boxes.

slides.say: And the last kind. A question that asks at most how many tries. Remember worst luck from topic twenty-one? We use it here.

Noa has four keys for four lockers. She doesn't know which key opens which locker. She never tries a key that she already knows doesn't fit. At most how many tries does she need to open all four? A try that opens a locker counts too.
The first locker. With the worst luck, the right key is the last one she tries. Three wrong keys, and then the right one. That's four tries.
That key is used now, so three keys are left for the second locker. With the worst luck, three tries.
Then two tries for the third locker, and one try for the last one.
at: one try for the last one

slides.say: Four plus three plus two plus one is ten tries.
at: Four plus three plus two plus one

slides.say: So let's sum it up. At least one is all, minus none.
When objects go into boxes, ask who chooses. Each object chooses a box.
And for at most how many tries, imagine the worst luck at every step. Take a moment to memorize this, and I'll see you in the next video.
